text: Hemp-Derived Hierarchical Porous Carbon with an Optimized Pore Structure by NaOH Activation for Supercapacitor Applications

This study focuses on converting hemp hurd, a byproduct of hemp stalk processing, into high-performance activated carbon for supercapacitor applications. Hemp hurd was pyrolyzed and subsequently activated with NaOH at various ratios (biochar:NaOH = 1:1, 1:2, 1:3, 1:4). The Hurd-4 condition (1:4 ratio) yielded the highest specific surface area, 3033 m 2 /g. Our findings indicate that increasing the chemical activation ratio enhances the mesopore-to-micropore volume ratio ( V meso / V micro ) to 1.58 while maintaining a sufficient micropore volume for ion storage. This balanced pore structure effectively increased the specific capacitance, achieving a maximum of 725 F/g at a current density of 0.3 A/g in a 1 M H 2 SO 4 electrolyte. When assembled into a coin cell with an organic electrolyte, Hurd-4 exhibited a maximum specific capacitance of 39 F/g, a maximum energy density of 34 Wh/kg, and a power density of 395 W/kg, surpassing commercial activated carbon. Additionally, the device maintained 78% capacitance retention after 10,000 cycles at a current density of 0.5 A/g. The superior electrochemical properties are attributed to the largest specific surface area, highest pore volume, and optimal mesopore volume ratio. These results demonstrate the potential of hemp hurd as a highly efficient precursor for synthesizing activated carbon for high-performance supercapacitors.
Introduction

Electrical energy generation by fossil fuels causes the production of greenhouse gases, leading to global warming, which has severe environmental impacts. Therefore, renewable energy sources as alternatives for electrical energy generation are attracting wide interest. Efficient and sustainable energy storage solutions are necessary for renewable energy in order to store excess energy and release energy when required. For renewable electrical energy applications that require many rapid charge/discharge cycles, such as regenerative braking, supercapacitors are considered one of the most promising energy storage devices due to their higher power density compared to batteries. − There are mainly three types of supercapacitors: electrical double-layer capacitors (EDLCs), pseudocapacitors, and hybrid supercapacitors. − Among these, EDLCs are the most commonly used due to their ability to have a fast charging time, high power density, long lifetime, environmental safety, and high specific capacitance. However, they have low energy density and a small voltage window; hence, there is a need to improve those properties.

Supercapacitors consist of two electrodes, a separator, and an electrolyte. Developing EDLCs with high specific capacitance, high energy density, and high power density requires electrodes with a large surface area, low resistance, and pore sizes suitable for the electrolyte. Carbon-based electrodes, such as activated carbon, carbon aerogels, and carbon nanotubes (CNTs), are being actively researched on because of their large surface area and high electrical conductivity. , Activated carbon is considered a viable choice due to its high surface area, high pore volume for ion adsorption, tunable pore sizes, electrochemical stability, multisource synthesis, and lower cost , as it can be synthesized from biomass or agricultural waste, such as green leaves, , bamboo, peanut shells, coconut shells, durian shells, corn cobs, and silkworm waste.

On the other hand, hemp ( Cannabis Sativa L.) gains attention for its economic viability, adaptability to various climates, ease of cultivation, and rapid growth. , Every part of the hemp stalk, including its fiber, leaves, flowers, and roots, can be used for products ranging from textiles and beverages to food, medicines, and cosmetics. However, this leaves substantial amounts of stem material as a byproduct, particularly the core part (hurd), which comprises 70–80% of the hemp stalk. The hemp hurds, despite possessing beneficial properties such as high absorbency and lightweight, remain underutilized. Therefore, maximizing the potential of hemp hurds to achieve zero waste presents both a challenge and an opportunity. Current applications being explored include construction materials, animal bedding, paper production, bioenergy, biocomposites, and soil remediation. One promising application is the conversion of hemp hurds into activated carbon for supercapacitor electrodes.

The process for synthesizing activated carbon involves the carbonization of biomass and activation. The carbonization of biomass can be achieved using three main techniques: hydrothermal process, which utilizes decomposition by steam at high pressure, dehydration, which utilizes the dehydration reaction with concentrated H 2 SO 4 , and pyrolysis, which uses thermal decomposition at high temperatures under inert gases. The activation can be done physically or chemically to create a larger surface area and a suitable pore structure in the carbon material. Typically, physical activation is performed using CO 2 gas and steam at high temperatures, while chemical activation uses chemical reagents, such as KOH, NaOH, and H 3 PO 4 , which can yield a larger surface area compared to physical activation.

Previous studies have extensively demonstrated that the structure and morphology of activated carbons depend not only on the carbonization and activation conditions but also on the intrinsic nature and lignocellulosic composition of the biomass precursor. − Synthesis parameters, including precursor composition, physical activation, and chemical activation, strongly influence pore size distribution, surface area, surface functional groups, and the overall structure. For instance, hemp, in particular, has been widely investigated as a raw material through different plant parts and synthesis strategies. Prior work has examined hydrothermal carbonization combined with KOH activation at varying ratios to produce activated carbons with tailored surface areas. ,,,− Hemp bast fiber has been used to fabricate interconnected carbon nanosheets via hydrothermal carbonization and KOH activation, achieving ultrafast supercapacitors with high energy density. Similarly, hemp fiber has been processed by one-step calcination with KOH to form porous carbon honeycomb structures for hybrid capacitors with enhanced electrochemical performance. Hemp-stem-derived activated carbon has also been synthesized by hydrothermal carbonization and KOH activation for aqueous zinc-ion hybrid supercapacitors. Raw hemp fibers (husk and bast) have been converted into activated carbon through pyrolysis and NaOH activation for aqueous supercapacitors.

Importantly, lignin has been identified as the predominant contributor to char and activated carbon formation. , Thus, targeting lignin-rich hemp hurd, the component with the highest lignin content among hemp parts, represents a promising route to maximize the electrochemical performance. However, it is worth noting that there is limited research on using hemp hurds as supercapacitor electrode materials via pyrolysis carbonization combined with NaOH activation. Literature reports indicate that while alkaline hydroxides, such as KOH ,, and NaOH, ,, are effective in producing activated carbon with a high specific surface area, NaOH offers potential advantages. Notably, NaOH activation can reduce both production costs and environmental impact compared to KOH. , Therefore, exploring NaOH as an alternative activating agent could enhance both the economic and environmental sustainability of the manufacturing process. Our previous work explored using raw hemp fibers (husk and bast mixed together as received after harvest) activated with NaOH as electrode materials for EDLCs in various electrolytes, with optimal performance observed in a H 2 SO 4 electrolyte. Building on this foundation, this study focuses on hemp hurd as the precursor, leveraging its high lignin content to enhance electrochemical performance after activation.

In this study, hemp hurds were converted into activated carbon electrodes for EDLCs using a two-step process: pyrolysis carbonization and NaOH activation. To optimize the pore structure and enhance the EDLC performance characteristics (specific capacitance, energy density, and power density), we investigated various weight ratios of biochar to NaOH (1:1 to 1:4). The physicochemical properties, specific surface area, and pore volume were characterized for each activation condition. The EDLC performance of the resulting materials was evaluated and compared with both biomass-derived activated carbons from the literature and commercial activated carbon commonly used in EDLCs.
Experimental Section
Materials

Hemp hurds as the raw material (Hurd-RM) were received from Eastern Spectrum Group Co., Ltd., Thailand. The hemp hurd was sourced from a hemp farm in the northern region of Thailand. NaOH (Carlo Erba, France), HCl (Q RëC, New Zealand), carbon black (Ketjenblack, Lion Specialty Chemicals, Japan), H 2 SO 4 (Q RëC, New Zealand), polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) (MTI, USA), and tetraethylammonium tetrafluoroborate (TEABF 4 ) (Osaka Chemical, Japan) were used as received without further purification. High-purity nitrogen (99.999%) and argon (99.999%) (S.I. Technology, Thailand) were also used. Activated carbon (AB520Y, MTI South Korea) was used as received for comparison.
Preparation of Activated Carbon

Hemp hurds were dried in an oven overnight to remove moisture. The dried hemp hurds were chopped into elongated and flat particles of size in the range of approximately 5–20 mm and were not ground before the pyrolysis process because hemp hurds are quite ductile and require a longer time to grind into smaller sizes. For pyrolysis carbonization, approximately 20 g of hemp hurds was heated to 500 °C with a temperature ramping rate of 5 °C/min under a nitrogen atmosphere with a flow rate of 500 sccm, and the mixture was kept at this temperature for 2 h. Here, the pyrolyzed product is denoted as hemp-hurd-derived biochar (Hurd-BC). The Hurd-BC was then ground into a powder by ball milling for 20 min at a frequency of 30 Hz. For activation, Hurd-BC was mixed with NaOH in different weight ratios (biochar:NaOH) of 1:1, 1:2, 1:3, and 1:4 using a mortar and then heated to 720 °C with a temperature ramping rate of 5 °C/min under an argon atmosphere with a flow rate of 500 sccm, and the mixture was kept at this temperature for 1 h. The activation temperature was chosen based on the optimized temperature from the previous research. ,, The activated products were washed by stirring at 300 rpm in a 1 M HCl solution at 100 °C for 4 h and subsequently rinsed in deionized water until the pH value became neutral. The rinsed products were collected by filtration and dried at 100 °C overnight. The samples are named Hurd- X , which is activated carbon by hemp hurds, and X is the weight ratio of NaOH ( X = 1, 2, 3, or 4) used in the activation step. The yield of the product is calculated as the ratio of the weight of the final product after activation to the weight of the dried hemp hurds before carbonization.
Characterization of Activated Carbon

The surface morphology of Hurd-RM was observed using environmental scanning electron microscopy (ESEM) (Quanta 250, FEI, USA) at an accelerated voltage of 10 kV. The surface morphology of biochar and activated carbons was characterized through field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) (SU5000, Hitachi, Japan) at an accelerated voltage of 10 kV. The internal structure of activated carbons was examined using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (JEM-2010, JEOL, Japan) at an accelerated voltage of 200 kV. The particle size of activated carbon was analyzed by a particle analyzer (Delsa Nano C, Beckman Coulter, USA). A Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometer (Spectrum Two FTIR Spectrometer, PerkinElmer, USA) was used to identify the functional groups of activated carbons within a wavenumber range of 500–4000 cm –1 . Additionally, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (Quantera II instrument, ULVAC-PHI, Japan) was employed to determine the chemical composition of the activated carbons. The chemical nature of the surface functionalities was further evaluated by Boehm titration using NaOH and HCl. The carbon crystal structure of biochar and activated carbons was analyzed by using Raman spectroscopy (DXR Smart Raman, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) with a laser wavelength of 532 nm, and X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were performed (SmartLab, Rigaku, Japan) using 1.2 kVA Cu K-α1 radiation. Additionally, XPS (Quantera II instrument, ULVAC-PHI, Japan) was employed to determine the chemical composition of activated carbons. The Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area, pore diameter, and pore volume of biochar and activated carbons were determined based on nitrogen adsorption/desorption at 77 K (Autosorb iQ-C-XR-XR-XR Quantachrome, USA).
Fabrication of Electrode and Electrochemical Measurements

EDLC electrodes were separately fabricated by using either hemp-hurd-derived activated carbons (hereinafter referred to as Hurd-ACs) or commercial activated carbon (AB520Y) as an ion adsorption material, combined with commercial carbon black as a conductive agent and PTFE as a binder. These components were mixed in a weight ratio of 90:5:5, respectively, and ground in a mortar and pestle for 3 min. The mixture was then milled and rolled to form an ultrathin carbon sheet (approximately 0.1 mm thickness). The sheet was punched into a circular shape with a diameter of approximately 10 mm and a weight of 4–8 mg to be used as EDLC electrodes. Electrochemical characterization of fabricated EDLC electrodes was conducted using both three- and two-electrode configurations. The three-electrode system employed platinum as the counter electrode, Ag/AgCl as the reference electrode, and 1 M H 2 SO 4 as the electrolyte. For the two-electrode configuration, a sandwich-type cell structure was assembled in a CR2032 coin cell using activated-carbon-based electrodes, a PTFE membrane separator, and TEABF 4 as the organic electrolyte.

Electrochemical characterization was performed using a Metrohm Autolab PGSTAT0302N instrument (Switzerland), employing cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) techniques. For the three-electrode configuration, CV measurements were conducted within a potential window of −0.1 to 0.9 V at scan rates ranging from 5 to 100 mV/s, while GCD measurements were performed between 0.0 and 1.0 V at current densities from 0.3 to 3.0 A/g. For the two-electrode configuration, both CV and GCD measurements were conducted within a potential window of 0.0 to 2.5 V, using the same scan rates and current densities as the three-electrode system. EIS measurements for both configurations were performed across a frequency range of 0.1 Hz to 0.1 MHz with an AC amplitude of 5 mV. Cycling stability was evaluated in the two-electrode configuration using GCD at a current density of 0.5 A/g within a potential window of 0.0 to 2.5 V.

Results and Discussion
Morphology and Structure Characterization

The hemp hurd chunks were yellowish, while the biochar and activated carbon turned black after undergoing pyrolysis carbonization and chemical activation.

Figure a displays an ESEM image depicting a typical plant cell wall, which includes various tracheary elements, such as elongated, rigid, and lignified xylem cells. Reticulate and pitted structures are clearly visible. Figure b presents an FE-SEM image of Hurd-BC, revealing irregularly shaped chips with relatively smooth and nonporous surfaces. Figure c–f presents the FE-SEM images of Hurd-ACs (Hurd-1, Hurd-2, Hurd-3, and Hurd-4), respectively. All samples exhibit a similar shape, resembling fractured rods. Notably, the rougher surfaces of Hurd-ACs compared to Hurd-BC indicate successful pore formation due to NaOH chemical activation. The differences in surface morphology among Hurd-ACs, associated with varying NaOH ratios, illustrate the role of NaOH as an activation agent. The higher NaOH ratio results in a more pronounced etching reaction between NaOH and carbon atoms, leading to increased porosity. The variations in NaOH activation ratios highlight the importance of optimizing the activation process for tailored material properties. However, it is important to consider the practical constraints of NaOH usage, as highlighted by the 1:4 biochar-to-NaOH ratio, which mitigates the risk of high corrosion and maintains a viable activated carbon yield. For comparison, Figure g presents an FE-SEM image of commercial activated carbon (AB520Y). AB520Y exhibits a lumpy structure with few surface pores, unlike the Hurd-ACs, suggesting that Hurd-ACs offer distinct advantages in terms of their porous nature. To confirm the pore formation in Hurd-ACs, TEM characterization of Hurd-4 is shown in Figure f . Small bright dots are dispersed throughout the area, implying micropore formation. The inset of each image in Figure corresponds to the low-magnification image of each sample. The particle size of activated carbon was analyzed by a particle analyzer (Delsa Nano C, Beckman Coulter, USA). The average sizes of Hurd-1, Hurd-2, Hurd-3, and Hurd-4 are approximately 6.20 ± 0.73, 5.54 ± 1.26, 3.39 ± 0.42, and 3.22 ± 0.26 μm, respectively, as shown in Figure S1 . The particle size of activated carbon tends to decrease as the amount of NaOH increases. For comparison, the commercial activated carbon (AB520Y) exhibited an average particle size of 3.02 ± 0.40 μm. The particle sizes obtained in this work are within a comparable range to those reported previously.

The surface functionalities of the Hurd-BC and Hurd-ACs were investigated using FTIR spectroscopy, as shown in Figure a. Hurd-BC and Hurd-ACs exhibited distinctly different characteristic peaks. Specifically, Hurd-BC showed no clear peaks corresponding to C–O, CO, and C–O–C groups, in contrast to the Hurd-ACs. However, this confirmed the presence of fundamental carbon backbone structures, including C–H stretching at ∼2900 cm – 1 and aromatic CC stretching at ∼1560 cm – 1 . To obtain quantitative information on the elemental composition and chemical states, XPS analysis was performed. The survey spectrum revealed the presence of carbon, oxygen, potassium, and chlorine in Hurd-BC, with potassium and chlorine likely originating from inorganic components naturally present in the biomass ( Figure b). In contrast, Hurd-ACs displayed only carbon and oxygen elements. Notably, sodium, potentially remaining as a residue of NaOH after activation, was not detected in Hurd-ACs. This absence of sodium can be attributed to the thorough washing process, during which the pH was adjusted to neutral using a 1 M HCl solution, followed by repeated rinsing with deionized water, effectively removing residual sodium-containing species.

Table shows the elemental composition and product yield of Hurd-BC, Hurd-ACs, and AB520Y. Hurd-BC has the lowest carbon content of 83.9%, while the carbon content of all Hurd-ACs is higher than that of Hurd-BC and is comparable to AB520Y. The product of the pyrolysis process is biochar (Hurd-BC) with a yield of 32.2%. After that, with successful chemical activation, the total yields of Hurd-1, Hurd-2, Hurd-3, and Hurd-4 are 17.8, 20.0, 15.4, and 11.4%, respectively. It can be seen that the product yield of Hurd-ACs is smaller with a higher mass ratio of NaOH, suggesting the effect of etching of the carbon structure by NaOH, as expected. Reduction in the oxygen content suggests the removal of oxygen-related functional groups from Hurd-ACs. However, the variation of mass ratio of NaOH seems to have very less effect on the change in carbon and oxygen content, possibly because the minimum amount of NaOH used in this experiment is already excessive for the oxygen removal effect, or the reaction may be dominated by mechanisms other than the chemical reaction with NaOH, such as thermal decomposition of oxygen-related bonds. Nevertheless, Hurd-4 shows the highest carbon concentration and ratio of carbon to oxygen elements (C/O).

To investigate the surface functional groups in greater detail, the narrow-scan spectra of C 1s and O 1s for Hurd-ACs and AB520Y were deconvoluted ( Figures and ). The C 1s spectra of all samples consistently revealed four main functional groups: C–C/CC (aromatic ring) (284.5 eV), C–OH (phenolic), or C–O–C (ether) (285.8 eV), CO (carbonyl) (287.8 eV), and CO (carboxyl) (290.0 eV), with C–C/CC being the most abundant in all cases. The concentrations of each carbon functional group for all samples are summarized in Table . Consistent with the C 1s narrow-scan spectra, the deconvoluted O 1s spectra of all samples revealed three predominant oxygen-containing functional groups: OC–OH (carboxyl) (531.0 eV), CO (carbonyl) (532.3 eV), and C–OH (phenolic) (533.8 eV). The relative concentrations of these groups are summarized in Table . These results are consistent with the FTIR observations, confirming that oxygen-containing functional groups were successfully introduced during the activation process.

The chemical nature of the surface functionalities was further assessed by Boehm titration using NaOH and HCl, which confirmed the presence of surface acidic groups (carboxylic, lactonic, and phenolic). The concentrations of total surface acidic groups on Hurd-1, Hurd-2, Hurd-3, Hurd-4, and AB520Y were approximately 1.42, 1.24, 1.12, 0.93, and 0.22 mmol/g, respectively. Notably, Hurd-ACs exhibited a higher content than commercial activated carbon. Overall, spectroscopic and titration analyses consistently highlight the abundance of oxygen-containing groups of Hurd-ACs, which are expected to improve electrode wettability and facilitate electrolyte accessibility within the porous structure. Nevertheless, an excessive amount of these groups may increase the electrical resistance of activated carbon, thereby potentially impairing its performance in supercapacitor applications.

Figure shows the Raman spectra of Hurd-BC, Hurd-ACs, and AB520Y. Defect-activated D band (∼1350 cm –1 ) and G band (∼1590 cm –1 ) were observed in all samples. Typically, the G band arises from the C–C stretching vibration in sp 2 -hybridized carbon systems, and the D band is attributed to the breathing modes of sp 2 carbon atoms in aromatic rings. , The degree of graphitization of carbon materials correlates with the intensity ratio between the G and D bands ( I G / I D ). Hurd-BC shows the highest I G / I D (1.47) compared to the other samples, suggesting minimal defect formation during carbonization. In contrast, Hurd-ACs show smaller I G / I D values compared with Hurd-BC, indicating the formation of defects as a result of NaOH activation. The I G / I D values of Hurd-1, Hurd-2, Hurd-3, and Hurd-4 were 1.03, 1.05, 1.06, and 1.09, respectively, which are higher than those of commercial activated carbon AB520Y ( I G / I D = 0.88). This indicates that Hurd-ACs possess a higher degree of crystallinity, which may contribute to the improved electrical conductivity. When comparing Hurd-BC and Hurd-X, the I G / I D clearly decreases. However, within the Hurd-X series, I G / I D shows a slight increase as the NaOH ratio increases. These results are not straightforward to explain. Nevertheless, based on previous reports, they can be understood as follows: NaOH activation can increase the I G / I D even as chemical etching generates greater porosity and apparent defect sites because I G / I D is also sensitive to domain size, amorphous content, and spectral broadening. In addition, alkali salts can catalyze local regraphitization, thereby modifying the Raman signature. Similar behavior has been reported for NaOH-activated hollow carbon shells, where I G / I D increased with higher NaOH content during in situ activation. Other salt-based or alkaline activation methods (e.g., seawater activation) have likewise shown enhanced graphitic character, reflected in higher I G / I D or increased graphitization under certain thermal and chemical conditions.

Generally, a stronger D band relative to the G band indicates a higher degree of disorder or more defect sites in the carbon structure. These defects can enhance ion adsorption by introducing active sites, which may correlate with increased specific surface area. However, a higher density of defects does not always equate to a larger accessible surface area. In some cases, defects may form within closed or multilayer-stacked regions, where ion diffusion and adsorption are limited. As a result, such internal defects may not significantly contribute to the usable surface area for electrochemical processes. Moreover, maintaining the electrical conductivity of the adsorption material is crucial as lower conductivity can result in a significant IR drop during charge–discharge cycles. As a trade-off, a large number of defects can increase the specific surface area but may reduce electrical conductivity and vice versa. Therefore, optimizing the specific surface area and electrical conductivity of the electrode material is crucial for enhancing the performance of EDLCs. The degree of graphitization and defect density, as indicated by Raman spectra, will be analyzed alongside the specific surface area and EDLC performance to develop a strategy for improving specific capacitance and energy density in EDLCs using biomass-derived activated carbon electrodes.

Figure b presents the XRD spectra of all samples in the 2θ range of 10°–70°, indicating a disordered carbon structure that lies between graphite and amorphous carbon. In Hurd-1, Hurd-2, Hurd-3, and AB520Y, a broad peak is observed at 24°, corresponding to the (002) plane of amorphous carbon, and another peak appears at 44°, associated with the (100) plane of graphite. However, Hurd-4 exhibited a broad diffraction peak in the 2θ range of approximately 23°–26°, suggesting the presence of a turbostratic graphite microcrystalline structure. Furthermore, the increased background intensity observed in the 2θ range of 10° to 20° is likely attributed to the presence of micropores, which induce X-ray scattering within the porous structure, thereby leading to an elevated background signal.

Figure a shows nitrogen adsorption–desorption isotherms of Hurd-BC, Hurd-ACs, and AB520Y, while the individual isotherm of Hurd-4 is provided in Figure S2 . All Hurd-ACs and AB520Y exhibit type IV isotherms with hysteresis loops in the relative pressure range of 0.2–1.0, according to the IUPAC classification, indicating the presence of mesoporous structures. Figure b presents the pore size distribution (PSD) of Hurd-BC, Hurd-ACs, and AB520Y, obtained from DFT calculations. Consistent with the type IV isotherm analysis, the pore size distribution of micro- and mesopores in Hurd-ACs and AB520Y falls within the range of 0.5–2.5 nm. In contrast, Hurd-BC exhibits no distinctive pore features. This suggests that micropores and mesopores are formed through the activation reaction with NaOH. The specific surface area, pore volume, and pore diameter of the samples are summarized in Table . As expected, the specific surface area and pore volume of Hurd-BC are significantly smaller than those of the Hurd-ACs. The specific surface areas of Hurd-1, Hurd-2, Hurd-3, and Hurd-4 are 2270, 2238, 2748, and 3033 m 2 /g, while their corresponding pore volumes are 0.99, 1.08, 1.29, and 1.55 cm 3 /g, respectively. Hurd-ACs exhibit a larger surface area and pore volume than AB520Y (1621 m 2 /g and 0.80 cm 3 /g). Additionally, increasing the NaOH ratio enhances the contribution of mesopores to the overall specific surface area and pore volume. This occurs because the reaction of NaOH with carbon, as shown in Equation , generates sodium atoms and H 2 gas within the Hurd-BC structure.

The subsequent removal of these species transforms micropores into meso- and macropores. The reaction also leads to the formation of carbon rods with numerous small pores on their surface, as observed in the SEM images ( Figure ). Although hemp hurds exhibit relatively weak carbon–carbon bonds after carbonization, activation with a 4-fold amount of NaOH helps preserve C–C bonding through the following mechanism. According to the literature, a portion of the generated sodium atoms may undergo secondary transformations, which further promote oxygen loss during activation. This enhanced oxygen removal likely facilitates carbon condensation and structural rearrangement. XPS analysis confirmed a slight increase in the relative content of sp 2 -hybridized carbon (C–C/CC) with higher NaOH ratios, indicating that deoxygenation promotes the development of more ordered carbon domains ( Table ). This interpretation is consistent with Raman spectroscopy results, which demonstrate a higher degree of graphitization in the synthesized Hurd-ACs compared with commercial activated carbon ( Figure a).

Hurd-4 exhibits the largest specific surface area (3033 m 2 /g) and the highest pore volume (1.55 cm 3 /g), surpassing values reported in previous studies, such as KOH-activated hemp-derived activated carbon with a specific surface area of 2446 m 2 /g and a total pore volume of 1.06 cm 3 /g. This could be due to the relatively smaller molecular size of NaOH, which facilitates a greater degree of diffusion into the biochar. Meanwhile, a comparative analysis between Hurd-4 with different materials, such as coal tar pitch (CTP)-derived porous carbon and Eucommia ulmoides (EUO) wood-derived activated carbon, highlights notable differences in porosity and electrochemical behavior, as summarized in Table S1 . While the microporous nature of Hurd-4 is comparable to that of CTP-based porous carbons, this study focuses on hemp as a renewable and sustainable biomass precursor. Notably, lignin has been identified as the predominant contributor to char and activated carbon formation. , By targeting hemp hurd, the hemp component with the highest lignin content, we demonstrate a promising route to maximize electrochemical performance while offering a significant environmental advantage over fossil-fuel-derived carbon. Our findings are also consistent with previous reports on biomass-derived mesoporous carbons, such as EUO-derived activated carbon, which emphasize the importance of biomass-derived precursors for synthesizing high-performance mesoporous carbon.

The surface area and pore volume are key factors in determining the ion transfer efficiency of the electrolyte and the specific capacitance of the EDLCs. This is because ions are transported and stored on the surface, while the pore volume influences the ion storage capacity within each pore. The second most important factor is the pore volume ratio between meso- and micropores. Mesopores facilitate ion transport into the pores, making them crucial, while micropores are responsible for ion retention. , Increasing the mesopore content while maintaining a sufficient number of micropores to optimize the specific surface area is key to achieving higher specific capacitance in EDLCs with activated-carbon-based electrodes. Among the characterized samples, Hurd-4 exhibits the largest specific surface area, the highest pore volume, and the greatest mesopore volume fraction.

Figure a presents CV curves measured in a three-electrode configuration within a voltage range of −0.1 to 0.9 V (a total potential window of 1.0 V) at a scan rate of 5 mV/s. The CV curves of Hurd-ACs and AB520Y exhibit a nearly rectangular shape, indicative of typical EDLC behavior. This suggests a rapid response to voltage changes and efficient ion transport during the charge and discharge processes. The CV curve of Hurd-ACs exhibits relatively less distortion compared with that of AB520Y, indicating that the EDLC behavior of Hurd-ACs is closer to ideal. The specific capacitance follows an increasing trend with a higher NaOH ratio, as evidenced by the larger CV curve area. Figure b presents the GCD curves measured at a current density of 0.3 A/g within a potential range of 0.0–1.0 V. All samples exhibit symmetric triangular curves with a nearly linear voltage response, indicating close-to-ideal charge and discharge behavior characteristic of EDLCs. The specific capacitance of each EDLC electrode, calculated from the GCD curves using eq , is as follows: Hurd-1 (518 F/g), Hurd-2 (576 F/g), Hurd-3 (603 F/g), Hurd-4 (725 F/g), and AB520Y (295 F/g). Hurd-4 exhibits the highest specific capacitance among the samples, as determined from GCD measurements in a three-electrode configuration, using 1 M H 2 SO 4 as the electrolyte. This value surpasses those reported in previous studies on electrodes based on hemp-derived activated carbons ,,− and aligns with the BET results shown in Figure . Hurd-4 is expected to exhibit the highest specific capacitance due to its largest specific surface area, highest pore volume, and greatest mesopore volume ratio among all measured samples, exceeding values reported in previous literature. − ,,,,,,,, A sample with an even higher NaOH ratio (Hurd-5) was also synthesized and characterized. However, it exhibited a lower mass yield than Hurd-4 without significant improvement in the specific surface area, pore volume, or specific capacitance. Therefore, its data are not presented. Next, the rate performance of the EDLC electrode based on Hurd-4 was evaluated. Figure c presents the CV curves of Hurd-4 at scan rates of 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 mV/s. As the scan rate increases, both the current density and specific capacitance decrease. However, even at 100 mV/s, the CV curve retains a semirectangular shape, indicating the high stability of the Hurd-4-based electrode. This also suggests a relatively uniform movement of electrons across the electrode surface. Figure d presents the GCD curves of Hurd-4 at current densities of 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0, and 10.0 A/g. The semisymmetrical triangular shape of the curves remains consistent even at the highest current density of 10.0 A/g, indicating stable charge–discharge behavior. The specific capacitance values calculated at 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0, and 10.0 A/g are 725, 538, 435, 268, and 151 F/g, respectively, further confirming the stability of the Hurd-4-based EDLC electrode. These results suggest that the high specific capacitance and stable rate performance of Hurd-4-based EDLC electrodes can be attributed to the specific surface area and mesopore volume fraction of activated carbon used.

In an ideal supercapacitor, the GCD curve exhibits a perfectly symmetrical triangular shape. This symmetry indicates that the charge and discharge processes involve equal amounts of charge, resulting in a Coulombic efficiency of 100%. In this work, a Coulombic efficiency of each electrode material at a current density of 0.3 A/g is summarized in Table S2 . Hurd-ACs show an efficiency comparable to that of AB520Y. A Coulombic efficiency of Hurd-4 at different current densities shows a clear increase with increasing current density. This improvement can be attributed to the fact that fast charge/discharge processes reduce the influence of slow ion diffusion, side reactions, and other irreversible processes, thereby making the stored and released charges more closely matched. As a result, Hurd-4 shows a Coulombic efficiency between 61 (0.3 A/g) and 94.9% (10.0 A/g) depending on the applied current density. These values are consistent with those commonly reported in related literature, as summarized in Table S2 .

Figure e illustrates the relationship between the specific surface area, specific capacitance, and mesopore-to-micropore volume ratio ( V meso / V micro ) to identify trends and optimal conditions. The results indicate that increasing the NaOH weight ratio during activation leads to a significant increase in both the V meso / V micro and specific capacitance. This suggests that the specific capacitance and rate performance of EDLCs with hurd-based activated carbon electrodes improve with increasing V meso / V micro while maintaining a sufficient amount of micropores to maximize the specific surface area. Notably, a biochar-to-NaOH mass ratio of 1:4 in the activation step was found to be optimal for achieving a well-balanced pore structure.

An appropriate distribution of micro-, meso-, and macropores is critical for high-performance carbon electrodes. Micropores primarily provide a large accessible surface area for charge storage, mesopores facilitate rapid ion transport and reduce diffusion resistance, and macropores act as ion-buffering reservoirs that shorten transport pathways. In our study, a V meso / V micro of 1.58 demonstrates that Hurd-4 possesses a hierarchical porous structure, where abundant mesopores enhance ion accessibility and improve charge–discharge kinetics. While a universally optimal ratio of micro/meso/macropores has not been established, since the ideal distribution can vary depending on the electrolyte system and electrode configuration, our results align well with the literature, which highlights that introducing sufficient mesoporosity is essential for balancing capacitance and rate performance. ,, The results also suggest that the optimal V meso / V micro ratio for achieving maximum specific capacitance with a 1 M H 2 SO 4 electrolyte is 1.58. In contrast, previous research on KOH-activated pecan-shell-based activated carbon, using a biochar-to-KOH mass ratio of 1:2 and 6 M KOH, reported an optimal V meso / V micro of 0.42 for maximum specific capacitance. This indicates that the ideal V meso /V micro ratio for maximizing specific capacitance in EDLCs using activated-carbon-based electrodes may vary depending on the electrolyte type or activation agent used. ,−

To further enhance the energy density, the organic electrolyte TEABF 4 was employed to extend the voltage window from 0.0–1.0 V (in a 1 M H 2 SO 4 electrolyte) to 0.0–2.5 V. Consequently, the electrochemical performance analysis of Hurd-ACs was conducted using a two-electrode sandwich coin cell with TEABF 4 as the electrolyte. Figure a presents the CV curves for EDLCs using either Hurd-ACs or AB520Y as electrodes at a scan rate of 5 mV/s. The CV curves of all samples retained their rectangular shape, indicating excellent ion transport behavior in the organic electrolyte. Figure b displays the GCD curves for Hurd-ACs at a current density of 0.3 A/g. The specific capacitances for Hurd-1, Hurd-2, Hurd-3, Hurd-4, and AB520Y were determined to be 29, 19, 38, 39, and 18 F/g, respectively. Despite the reduction in specific capacitance observed with the TEABF 4 electrolyte compared to 1 M H 2 SO 4 , samples with larger specific surface areas and higher mesopore-to-micropore volume ratios still exhibited superior capacitance. This confirms that, beyond simply increasing specific surface area, an optimal mesopore-to-micropore ratio is crucial for enhancing the specific capacitance of EDLCs using activated-carbon-based electrodes. Figure c presents the Nyquist plots from EIS measurements of Hurd-ACs over a frequency range of 0.1 Hz–0.1 MHz with an AC potential amplitude of 5 mV. The EIS analysis reveals two distinct regions: (1) a semicircle in the high-frequency region representing the series resistance ( R S ) and charge transfer resistance ( R CT ) and (2) a near-vertical line in the low-frequency region indicative of Warburg impedance. The equivalent circuit model corresponding to the EIS spectra is shown in the inset of Figure c. The extracted R S values from the X-intercept of the high-frequency region for Hurd-1, Hurd-2, Hurd-3, Hurd-4, and AB520Y are 2.2, 2.9, 4.8, 3.5, and 4.5 Ω, respectively. The corresponding extracted R CT values from the diameter of the semicircle are 7.0, 9.0, 3.0, 22.0, and 37.0 Ω, respectively. Notably, there is a discrepancy between R CT and specific capacitance, as lower R CT is typically expected in EDLCs with higher specific capacitance. However, in this study, activated carbon with a higher micropore volume exhibited a lower R CT . From Table , the micropore volume decreases in the following order: Hurd-3 > Hurd-1 > Hurd-2 > Hurd-4 > AB520Y. The high R CT observed in Hurd-4 can be attributed to the use of an electrolyte with ion sizes incompatible with its pore structure, resulting in inefficient ion infiltration, particularly into the micropores. This highlights a critical consideration in optimizing the specific capacitance of EDLCs with AC electrodes in organic electrolytes. Figure d displays the CV curves at scan rates of 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 mV/s for Hurd-4 in a coin cell within the potential range of 0.0–2.5 V. It can be observed that at a scan rate of 100 mV/s, the CV curve of Hurd-4 maintains a semirectangular shape, indicating adequate rate stability in the TEABF 4 electrolyte. Figure e presents the GCD curves at current densities of 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 3.0, and 5.0 A/g. The curves maintain a semisymmetrical triangular shape up to a current density of 5.0 A/g, indicating good capacitive behavior. The specific capacitance values calculated from the GCD curves at 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 3.0, and 5.0 A/g are 39, 38, 36, 31, and 30 F/g, respectively. The specific capacitance of Hurd-4 at a current density of 5.0 A/g retains 78% of its value compared to that at 0.3 A/g. The energy density and power density at 0.3 A/g, calculated using eqs and , are 34 Wh/kg and 395 W/kg, respectively. Cyclic stability testing was then performed by analyzing the charge–discharge behavior over 10,000 cycles at a current density of 0.5 A/g, as shown in Figure f. The Hurd-4 device exhibited a 78% retention rate, with its specific capacitance decreasing from 28 to 22 F/g after 10,000 cycles. Compared to AB520Y, Hurd-4 demonstrated a higher initial specific capacitance and a higher retention percentage after 10,000 cycles.

Tafel analysis is commonly used to characterize the charge-transfer kinetics of Faradaic reactions under quasi-steady-state conditions. In our case, the oxygen functional groups present on the carbon surface may contribute to pseudocapacitive redox processes, in addition to double-layer charging. For this reason, a pseudo-Tafel analysis was performed using CV data at a scan rate of 5 mV/s, focusing on the potential region where the current exhibits exponential behavior to extract the Faradaic component. Figure S3 shows the resulting Tafel plots for half-cells based on Hurd-4 and AB520Y, as well as for a full-cell based on Hurd-4. The anodic and cathodic Tafel slopes of the Hurd-4 half-cell were 36.6 and 44.9 mV/dec, respectively, compared with 67.0 and 95.6 mV/dec for AB520Y in a 1 M H 2 SO 4 electrolyte. The lower Tafel slopes of Hurd-4, which contains oxygen heteroatoms, indicate that surface Faradaic reactions associated with oxygen functionalities facilitate more efficient charge-transfer processes, thereby enhancing the pseudocapacitive response. However, because the electrode simultaneously exhibits double-layer capacitance, the extracted slopes should be regarded as apparent kinetic indicators rather than intrinsic reaction parameters. In the full-cell configuration with the TEABF 4 electrolyte, the anodic and cathodic Tafel slopes of Hurd-4 were 49.5 and 92.3 mV/dec, respectively. These higher slopes likely arise from the greater resistance of the organic electrolyte and from the fact that, in a full cell, both electrodes contribute to the overall polarization; the measured values therefore also include ohmic and transport resistances associated with the separator and electrolyte.

The energy density and power density of Hurd-4 in the TEABF 4 electrolyte, as determined from GCD at various current densities, are presented in Figure a. At a current density of 0.3 A/g, the energy density and power density are 34 Wh/kg and 395 W/kg, respectively. These values decrease to 33 Wh/kg and 689 W/kg at 0.5 A/g, 31 Wh/kg and 1561 W/kg at 1.0 A/g, and 27 Wh/kg and 8222 W/kg at 3.0 A/g. Despite suboptimal R CT and cyclic stability, the maximum energy density and power density achieved by Hurd-4 in this study are significantly higher than those of commercial activated carbon, up to twice as high, and exceed values reported in other studies. ,,,− For example, activated carbon derived from hemp stem exhibited an energy density of 19.8 Wh/kg and a power density of 21 kW/kg. This indicates that increasing V meso / V micro while maintaining a sufficient amount of micropores to maximize the specific surface area of activated carbon is an effective strategy to enhance the specific capacitance, rate performance, and energy density of EDLCs by using biomass-derived activated carbon electrodes. However, as shown in Figure b, analyzing the structural and electrochemical properties makes it challenging to clearly distinguish the factors that significantly influence the specific capacitance. The radar plot in Figure b illustrates the relationship between the material properties and supercapacitor performance. The evaluated properties include pore diameter, the volume ratio between mesopores and micropores ( V meso / V micro ), the volume ratio between mesopores and total pores ( V meso / V total ), the surface area ratio between mesopores and total pores ( S meso / S total ), total specific surface area (SSA), I G / I D , and the elemental ratio of carbon to other elements existing in the sample, all of which influence specific capacitance. From both material science and electrochemical perspectives, Hurd-4 demonstrates the best performance, exhibiting the largest enclosed area.

Conclusions

In summary, hemp-hurd-derived activated carbons (Hurd-ACs) were successfully synthesized through pyrolysis carbonization and NaOH activation (NaOH weight ratios = 1, 2, 3, and 4). It was found that EDLC electrodes fabricated under all conditions exhibited higher specific capacitance and surface area than commercial activated carbon (AB520Y). Among them, Hurd-4 (1:4) achieved the largest specific surface area of 3033 m 2 /g and the highest specific capacitance of 725 F/g in a 1 M H 2 SO 4 electrolyte, attributed to its largest specific surface area, highest pore volume, and greatest mesopore volume ratio among all samples. It was observed that increasing the NaOH weight ratio in the activation process significantly enhanced both V meso / V micro and specific capacitance. The findings suggest that the specific capacitance and rate performance of EDLCs using hurd-derived activated-carbon-based electrodes were optimized at V meso / V micro = 1.58, making them highly suitable for supercapacitor applications. Finally, the Hurd-4 coin cell in an organic electrolyte exhibited a maximum specific capacitance of 39 F/g, an energy density of 34 Wh/kg, and a power density of 395 W/kg.
